newsitem.title: USA: U.S. insurers seek passage to India.
newsitem.headline: U.S. insurers seek passage to India.

text.p: An increasing number of U.S. insurers view India as the most promising market in fast-growing Asia.

They say that the subcontinent offers easier access and better near-term growth potential than bigger, more ballyhooed China, because of its large middle class, English-style legal system and other factors.
But they concede that India is also saddled with political uncertainties and an entrenched bureaucracy.
"India is a top priority for us in terms of market development," said Kingsley Schubert, president of Philadelphia-based CIGNA Corp 's international arm.
CIGNA is among the handful of foreign insurers that have opened representative offices in India. None has been granted a government license to write business yet.

India has promised to open up its state-run insurance industry to foreign investors but has yet to specify a timetable. Healthcare insurance and pension services are expected to be the first two areas to be liberalized.
Schubert told Reuters he expects CIGNA to be among the first foreign licensees in India, and foreign insurers might be writing business there in early 1998.
He said India's recent change in government leadership should not pose a setback to the insurance liberalization process.

The country's health insurance market is worth an estimated $4.1 billion and is growing at a rate of 30 percent a year, according to a report by Winconsult Asia-Pacific, a subsidiary of Switzerland-based Winterthur Insurance Co.
Schubert said India held more immediate promise than China for several reasons.
First, the business licenses being dangled to foreign insurers are national in scope -- rather than limited to a metropolitan area or province, as in China.
In addition, "The legal environment in India is much more transparent and much more established," Schubert said.
"The overall middle class in India probably is at this stage more substantial than in China, and growing more rapidly."
Life and non-life insurance are already established concepts to India's middle class of up to 300 million people.

"It's a fairly sophisticated country, of what we think of as the poor, but they have this huge middle class," said William Berkley, chairman and chief executive of Greenwich, Connecticut-based insurer W.R. Berkley Corp.
"There is advertising for auto insurance all over. The concept of insurance is well thought-of," Berkley said.
"I think it's one of the better opportunities (in Asia), and when you look at it vis a vis China, you can feel a little more certain. Because the legal system (is based on English law)."
Aetna Inc and Chubb Corp are among the other U.S. insurers keen to write business in India.
"It's a great opportunity for us in India," said Frederick C. Copeland, Jr., president of Aetna International.
"The combination of economic growth, high population, low penetration and a growing middle class, are what typically is right for our business."

Aetna is in talks with prospective Indian partners to open a joint venture. "Our primary interest is in life and health," Copeland said. "There's a great deal of interest in the upper middle class in developing savings-oriented accounts which can then be managed by financial fiduciaries.

"India is a complex country, and has tended to lag the rest of Asia in terms of its own development. But it's also a country where there's a great deal of economic activity. So I think there's a real need for sponsor-based, insurance-style programs."
((--Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224))
